title: AP Human Geography
summary: Read spatial evidence and explain population, culture, land use and development patterns.
frameworkNote: 2026–27 structure checked against College Board on 15 October 2026: 7 units. Original VertexED focused lessons and self-check questions sample each unit; they do not replace the full course framework, required materials or teacher review.

modules.title: Scale, maps and spatial questions
modules.focus: Explain how aggregation changes the story a map tells.
explanation: Geographers examine where activities occur and why spatial patterns emerge. Absolute location uses a fixed reference; relative location describes connections. A place’s accessibility may change even when its coordinates remain constant.

Maps select and simplify. Scale, projection, boundaries and classification affect interpretation. A national average can hide neighbourhood differences, so evaluate whether the spatial unit matches the question before drawing conclusions about individuals.

workedExample.prompt: A country has a high average income but some districts have low incomes. Interpret both maps.
steps: The national map summarises the whole country.
The district map reveals uneven distribution that the aggregate conceals.

misconception.claim: Every resident has the average value shown for a region.
misconception.correction: Regional statistics do not determine individual characteristics.

questions.prompt: Why might a railway alter a town’s relative location?
questions.answer: It can connect the town more closely to markets and jobs by reducing travel time without moving its coordinates.

questions.prompt: What is lost when neighbourhood data are combined into one city value?
questions.answer: Contrasts among neighbourhoods can disappear, concealing clusters of deprivation or advantage.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical district has average income 30,000 credits. Explain why a map of this figure cannot establish that every household earns 30,000.
hints: An average summarises a distribution.
Household values can differ above and below it.
questions.answer: The district mean combines different household incomes, so individuals may earn much more or less. Household-level data or distributional measures are needed; assigning the mean to every household commits an ecological fallacy.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical analysts redraw neighbourhood boundaries around the same residents and obtain a different pattern of average unemployment. Explain how this can happen without anyone changing employment status.
questions.hint: The observations stay fixed but groupings change.
hints: The observations stay fixed but groupings change.
Rates depend on each area’s numerator and denominator.
questions.answer: New boundaries regroup employed and unemployed residents into different denominators, changing area rates and visible clusters. This illustrates sensitivity to spatial aggregation; it does not require an underlying employment change.

notes.title: Aggregation changes the visible pattern
paragraphs: A map’s scale of analysis is the spatial level at which data are studied, while cartographic scale relates map distance to ground distance. Changing analytical boundaries can change averages and apparent correlations even when underlying observations stay the same. This is part of the modifiable areal unit problem. A further error occurs when a group-level pattern is assigned to every individual, known as an ecological fallacy. Compare several relevant scales and inspect within-area variation before explaining a pattern. No projection preserves every property of Earth’s curved surface, so select the map according to the question rather than treating all visual distortions as equivalent.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical city: one neighbourhood has mean commute 10 minutes and another 40, with equal numbers of travellers. Find the city mean and assess “everyone commutes 25 minutes”.
steps: The equally weighted mean is (10 + 40)/2 = 25 minutes.
Neither neighbourhood mean equals 25, and individual journeys can vary further.
workedExamples.conclusion: The city average summarises the population; assigning it to every resident is an ecological inference error.

flashcards.back: The spatial level used to study a pattern.
The relation between map distance and ground distance.
Inferring individual characteristics directly from group-level data.

flashcards.front: Why can changing boundaries alter a map pattern?
flashcards.back: Different aggregation combines observations in different ways.

diagrams.title: Aggregation changes the visible pattern
diagrams.description: An overall mean can conceal strong local contrasts.

modules.title: Population change and migration
modules.focus: Separate natural increase from movements across boundaries.
explanation: Population change combines births, deaths, immigration and emigration. Natural increase excludes migration. Age structure influences future change because different cohorts contribute differently to births, work and demand for services.

Migration decisions reflect interacting pressures, opportunities, networks and barriers. A population pyramid with a broad young base suggests potential future growth, but policy, health and fertility changes affect what actually happens.

workedExample.prompt: A town records 900 births, 500 deaths, 300 arrivals and 450 departures.
steps: Natural increase is 900 − 500 = 400.
Net migration is −150, so total population increases by 250.

misconception.claim: A growing population must have positive net migration.
misconception.correction: Births exceeding deaths can offset net emigration.

questions.prompt: A region has 120 births, 100 deaths and net migration of −35. What is its change?
questions.answer: Natural increase is 20, so total change is −15 people.

questions.prompt: How can an established migrant network encourage further migration?
questions.answer: It can provide job information, housing contacts and practical support, reducing uncertainty for later migrants.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical region has 200,000 people, 1000 km² total land and 250 km² arable land. Calculate both arithmetic and physiological density and interpret the difference.
questions.hint: Use the same population with each area.
hints: Use the same population with each area.
Keep the land denominator in the interpretation.
questions.answer: Arithmetic density is 200 people/km² total land; physiological density is 800 people/km² arable land. The higher latter value reflects the smaller arable denominator, not an extra population.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical country’s fertility rate falls but its population continues growing because many people are entering childbearing ages. Explain the mechanism without assuming migration.
questions.hint: Numbers of potential parents matter as well as births per parent.
hints: Numbers of potential parents matter as well as births per parent.
Compare cohort size with the individual fertility trend.
questions.answer: A large reproductive-age cohort can produce many births even at a lower fertility rate. If births still exceed deaths, natural increase continues; this age-structure effect is population momentum.

notes.title: The land denominator changes the density measure
paragraphs: Population density has several denominators, each answering a different geographical question. Arithmetic density divides total population by total land area. Physiological density divides population by arable land area and can indicate pressure relative to potential cropland, while agricultural density compares farmers with arable land. None directly measures food security, which also depends on yields, trade, affordability and distribution. Demographic change likewise needs more than a single rate: a large cohort entering reproductive ages can sustain growth even as fertility falls. State the population, land definition and interval before comparing places or inferring future pressure.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical region has 600,000 people, 3000 km² total land and 600 km² arable land. Calculate arithmetic and physiological density.
steps: Arithmetic density = 600,000/3000 = 200 people/km² total land.
Physiological density = 600,000/600 = 1000 people/km² arable land.
workedExamples.conclusion: The second value is higher because the denominator is smaller; it does not alone prove food shortage.

flashcards.front: What denominator does arithmetic density use?
flashcards.back: Total land area.

flashcards.front: What denominator does physiological density use?
flashcards.back: Arable land area.
Farmers relative to arable land area.
Growth associated with age structure that can persist after fertility declines.

diagrams.title: The land denominator changes the density measure
diagrams.description: The same population can produce different valid density values.

edges.label: divide by all land for one measure
use cropland for a different question

modules.title: Culture, diffusion and landscapes
modules.focus: Identify how ideas spread without assuming cultures are fixed.
explanation: Culture includes learned practices, meanings and identities that change through interaction. Relocation diffusion moves practices with people; contagious diffusion spreads through nearby contact; hierarchical diffusion spreads through influential centres or groups.

A cultural landscape records human activity in buildings, language, sacred places and land use. These features can reflect power and adaptation, but one visible marker cannot establish every resident’s identity or beliefs.

workedExample.prompt: Migrants establish a familiar food tradition in a new city, then neighbouring communities adopt it.
steps: Migration first carries the practice through relocation diffusion.
Subsequent local contact can produce contagious diffusion.

misconception.claim: Cultural exchange always eliminates the original practice.
misconception.correction: Practices may persist, combine or change selectively.

questions.prompt: A fashion spreads from major cities to smaller cities through influencers. Which diffusion is emphasised?
questions.answer: Hierarchical diffusion, because influential centres shape adoption across a ranked network.

questions.prompt: Why is a multilingual street sign evidence of a cultural landscape?
questions.answer: It makes language communities and institutional choices visible in the built environment.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical migrants retain their home language while adopting some local workplace customs. Explain why this demonstrates selective acculturation rather than necessarily complete assimilation.
hints: Several practices can coexist.
One adopted custom does not establish loss of all distinct practices.
questions.answer: They adopt some practices through contact but retain a distinct language practice. This supports selective acculturation; complete assimilation is not established by the limited evidence.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical festival combines musical instruments from two traditions into a newly developed performance. Identify a relevant cultural process and distinguish it from simple relocation.
questions.hint: The traditions are combined rather than merely moved unchanged.
hints: The traditions are combined rather than merely moved unchanged.
Describe the new form.
questions.answer: The combination illustrates cultural syncretism because elements form a new performance. Relocation diffusion would emphasise people carrying an existing practice to a new place; it does not alone describe this blending.

notes.title: An idea can spread through local adaptation
paragraphs: Cultural interaction can produce adoption, adaptation or combination rather than a single uniform outcome. Acculturation involves adopting some practices through contact, while assimilation involves more extensive incorporation into another culture and possible loss of distinct practices. Syncretism combines elements into a new form. These processes can overlap and vary between people, generations and settings. Stimulus diffusion spreads an underlying idea that is adapted locally rather than copying its original form exactly. Evidence should identify the practice and the pathway of change, avoiding an assumption that one food, building or language choice reveals an entire community’s identity.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical food business adopts a foreign fast-service format but replaces its ingredients with locally preferred vegetarian foods. Identify a diffusion process.
steps: The organisational idea spreads, but the original menu is not copied unchanged.
Local adaptation of the underlying format illustrates stimulus diffusion.
workedExamples.conclusion: The example does not establish that customers have abandoned their wider cultural identities.

flashcards.back: An underlying idea spreads while its form is adapted locally.
The combination of cultural elements into a new form.

flashcards.front: Does adoption of one practice establish assimilation?
flashcards.back: No; broader identity and practices may persist.

flashcards.front: Why specify the pathway of diffusion?
flashcards.back: Movement by people, contact and influential networks are different mechanisms.

diagrams.title: An idea can spread through local adaptation
diagrams.description: The format travels while local preferences change its expression.

nodes.label: New expression
nodes.detail: Format retained without copying every original practice

edges.label: changes the form while retaining the idea

modules.title: Territory, identity and governance
modules.focus: Distinguish a nation from a sovereign state.
explanation: A state governs territory through political institutions; a nation is a community connected by a shared identity. Nations and state borders do not always coincide. A multinational state contains several national communities.

Boundaries can divide cultural groups or enclose diverse populations. Federalism distributes authority territorially; devolution transfers powers from a central government. Neither guarantees harmony, because resources, representation and identity still shape conflict.

workedExample.prompt: A state grants an elected regional assembly authority over education.
steps: Identify a transfer of decision-making power to a territorial level.
Describe it as devolution; do not infer independence or sovereignty.

misconception.claim: Every nation has its own independent state.
misconception.correction: Some nations cross borders or lack a sovereign state.

questions.prompt: Why might a border create difficulties for a pastoral community?
questions.answer: It can restrict movement between grazing areas or require permits where seasonal routes previously crossed freely.

questions.prompt: How can federalism accommodate regional differences?
questions.answer: Regional governments can make some policies suited to local needs while sharing national institutions, depending on constitutional powers.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical border closes a route used to reach seasonal grazing. Explain a geographical consequence and why the community’s identity need not change immediately.
hints: Separate movement restrictions from identity.
The political boundary changes access.
questions.answer: The closure can interrupt seasonal grazing and require longer routes or permits, affecting livelihoods. It does not automatically erase the community’s existing shared identity or cross-border relationships.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical region gains authority over schools but cannot conduct foreign policy. Evaluate the claim that it has become an independent sovereign state.
questions.hint: Identify the scope of transferred powers.
hints: Identify the scope of transferred powers.
Internal administration differs from external sovereignty.
questions.answer: The evidence shows limited regional self-government, not complete sovereign authority. Retained central foreign-policy power and the stated boundaries of education authority make an independence claim unsupported.

notes.title: Regional authority can recognise local preferences
paragraphs: Political boundaries can become barriers, meeting points or objects of dispute. Their effects depend on enforcement, transport links and the communities they cross. Centripetal forces encourage cohesion within a state, while centrifugal forces increase division; these are analytical categories rather than fixed properties of an ethnic or linguistic group. A shared institution may unite some residents while excluding others. Territorial autonomy can accommodate regional preferences, but the outcome depends on powers, resources and legitimacy. Distinguish sovereignty from administrative authority: regional decision-making does not by itself establish an independent state or control over external relations.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical multilingual state funds local-language schooling through regional governments while retaining national defence authority. Analyse the arrangement and one possible cohesion effect.
steps: Education authority is distributed territorially, while defence remains central.
Recognition of language preferences may reduce exclusion and support cohesion if access and resources are credible.
workedExamples.conclusion: The policy does not by itself create sovereign regional states or guarantee harmony.

flashcards.back: A factor encouraging political cohesion.
A factor encouraging political division.
No; powers may remain bounded within the state.

flashcards.front: Why avoid labelling a group inherently divisive?
flashcards.back: Effects depend on institutions, treatment and context.

diagrams.title: Regional authority can recognise local preferences
diagrams.description: A policy may support cohesion without transferring sovereignty.

nodes.label: Possible cohesion effect
nodes.detail: Recognition may reduce exclusion under suitable conditions

edges.label: inform the design of regional powers
can strengthen acceptance of the shared state

modules.title: Agriculture, markets and rural land
modules.focus: Use transport costs to explain a simplified land-use pattern.
explanation: Agricultural choices depend on climate, soils, labour, technology, policy and markets. Commercial and subsistence production differ in primary purpose, but households may combine sales with food grown for their own use.

A simplified market-distance model predicts that perishable or expensive-to-transport goods locate closer to a market. Its assumptions must be checked: refrigeration, multiple markets and uneven terrain can alter the pattern.

workedExample.prompt: Compare fresh milk and durable grain around one isolated market with equal land conditions.
steps: Milk’s perishability and transport demands favour nearby production in the model.
Grain can travel farther, though real technology and market networks can change this arrangement.

misconception.claim: A land-use model predicts every farm’s actual location.
misconception.correction: Models isolate relationships under assumptions and require adaptation to real conditions.

questions.prompt: How could refrigeration alter the distance fresh food travels?
questions.answer: Reduced spoilage allows longer journeys, weakening the need to produce immediately beside consumers.

questions.prompt: Why can export farming increase income yet create food-security concerns?
questions.hint: Consider what land produces and who can buy food.
questions.answer: Export earnings may rise while land shifts from local staples and households become dependent on volatile prices or purchased food.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical crop rents are X = 90 − 3d and Y = 60 − d. Find the crossover distance and which crop bids more at d = 10.
hints: Set the rent expressions equal.
Evaluate both at ten kilometres.
questions.answer: The crossover solves 30 = 2d, so d = 15 km. At d = 10, X offers 60 and Y offers 50 credits per hectare; X is the higher bidder.
checkpoints: X higher at the specified site.

questions.prompt: A new refrigerated route reduces spoilage for a perishable crop far from a market. Explain why its observed location might diverge from the original simple ring model.
questions.hint: Refrigeration changes a cost that rose with distance.
hints: Refrigeration changes a cost that rose with distance.
The original assumptions no longer match conditions.
questions.answer: Reduced spoilage lowers the crop’s distance-related costs, allowing profitable production farther away. The original ring prediction changes because its transport-cost assumptions have changed, rather than because location has no economic explanation.

notes.title: Different transport costs change the highest bidder
paragraphs: Agricultural location models compare the return available from different land uses after transport and production costs. Bid rent is the amount a producer can afford to pay for land while meeting the model’s other costs and return requirements. With one market and otherwise uniform conditions, a crop whose transport costs rise steeply with distance loses land-rent potential more quickly. The highest bidder may change with distance, producing rings in a simplified model. Real landscapes depart from this pattern because terrain, roads, multiple markets, refrigeration and policy alter costs. Use the model to explain a mechanism, not to force every farm into an ideal ring.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical bid-rent functions are A = 100 − 4d and B = 70 − d, where d is kilometres from a market and rents are credits per hectare. Find the crossover.
steps: Set 100 − 4d = 70 − d, giving 30 = 3d and d = 10 km.
At 5 km A offers 80 and B 65; at 15 km A offers 40 and B 55.
workedExamples.conclusion: A outbids B nearer the market; B outbids A beyond 10 km within this model’s valid range.

flashcards.back: The land payment a user can afford under specified revenue and cost conditions.

flashcards.front: Why can perishable goods favour nearby sites?
flashcards.back: Distance can raise spoilage and transport costs.

flashcards.front: What does a steeply falling rent curve indicate?
flashcards.back: Returns are highly sensitive to market distance.

flashcards.front: Name an assumption limiting simple agricultural rings.
flashcards.back: One market and otherwise uniform land and transport conditions.

diagrams.title: Different transport costs change the highest bidder
diagrams.description: The crop with the steeper decline loses its advantage farther from market.

edges.label: distance reduces A’s rent more rapidly

modules.title: Urban growth and unequal access
modules.focus: Connect land values, transport and housing opportunities.
explanation: Urban land use reflects accessibility, planning, investment and social power. Central locations often offer valuable connections, but employment may also cluster in suburbs or multiple centres. No single city model fits every place.

Gentrification can bring investment and improved services while rising rents displace lower-income residents. Evaluate effects by asking who benefits, who bears costs and whether residents retain access to housing and transport.

workedExample.prompt: A new transit station shortens commuting time and nearby rents rise.
steps: Improved accessibility can increase demand for nearby housing.
Higher rents may benefit owners while placing pressure on tenants with fixed incomes.

misconception.claim: Urban improvement benefits all residents equally.
misconception.correction: Benefits and costs depend on tenure, income and access to services.

questions.prompt: Why might a cheaper home far from jobs still be costly for a household?
questions.answer: Longer journeys can raise transport spending and time burdens, offsetting lower housing costs.

questions.prompt: What evidence could test whether regeneration displaced residents?
questions.answer: Rent changes, eviction records and resident relocation data can show displacement; new buildings alone cannot.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical largest city has 8 million residents. Under exact rank-size, predict the fourth-ranked city and state one reason the observed value could differ.
hints: Divide by the rank.
Historical or political concentration can alter the pattern.
questions.answer: The predicted fourth-city population is 8/4 = 2 million. Actual settlement may differ because of historical investment, political concentration or other processes, and the model is not a universal law.

questions.prompt: A report compares one city’s administrative population with another city’s metropolitan population and ranks them. Explain the comparability problem and a correction.
questions.hint: The boundaries include different kinds of territory.
hints: The boundaries include different kinds of territory.
Choose a shared definition.
questions.answer: The metropolitan count can include suburbs and surrounding settlements excluded by a city-proper count. Recalculate both using comparable administrative or metropolitan definitions before ranking their populations.

notes.title: Rank-size is a model of a settlement system
paragraphs: Urban settlement systems can be compared using rank and population size. The rank-size rule is an ideal pattern in which the city ranked n has about one-nth the population of the largest city. A primate city is disproportionately dominant relative to other cities and may concentrate political, economic or cultural functions. Neither pattern alone establishes a city’s quality of life or the fairness of resource distribution. Definitions of city boundaries matter: administrative city populations may differ from metropolitan populations. Apply one consistent definition before calculating ratios, then connect the pattern to historical and economic processes with additional evidence.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical urban system has a largest city of 6 million people. Under an exact rank-size model, predict the second, third and fourth city sizes.
steps: Predicted sizes are 6/2 = 3 million and 6/3 = 2 million.
The fourth is 6/4 = 1.5 million.
workedExamples.conclusion: These are model predictions, not observed populations or proof of a desirable settlement pattern.

flashcards.front: What does the rank-size rule predict for rank n?
flashcards.back: Approximately the largest city’s population divided by n.
A city disproportionately dominant within its urban system.

flashcards.front: Does primacy alone prove poor living conditions?
flashcards.back: No; outcomes need separate evidence.
City-proper and metropolitan boundaries produce different populations.

diagrams.title: Rank-size is a model of a settlement system
diagrams.description: Predicted population falls as city rank increases.

edges.label: divide the largest population by two
divide the largest population by three

modules.title: Development and production networks
modules.focus: Distinguish output, well-being and unequal connections.
explanation: Economic development includes changes in production and living conditions. GDP measures output; health, education and distribution reveal other dimensions. High average output can coexist with uneven access to opportunities and services.

Global production divides tasks across locations according to costs, skills, infrastructure and policy. A factory’s place in a supply chain affects wages and bargaining power, while relocation can expose workers to decisions made elsewhere.

workedExample.prompt: Two regions have equal GDP per person but different school attendance and life expectancy.
steps: Output per person alone ranks them equally.
Social indicators show that similar output does not imply equivalent living conditions.

misconception.claim: Economic growth and human development are identical.
misconception.correction: Growth can support development, but distribution and public choices influence its effects.

questions.prompt: Why might firms cluster near specialised suppliers?
questions.answer: Proximity can lower transaction and transport costs and improve access to skilled labour and knowledge.

questions.prompt: Why should a development comparison include gender differences?
questions.answer: National averages can conceal unequal access to education, work or political participation, limiting understanding of development.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical cluster membership saves a firm 12 units in supplier costs and 6 in recruitment, but adds 10 in rent. Find the net cost effect.
hints: Add both savings.
Subtract the additional cost.
questions.answer: Total savings are 18 units and extra rent is 10, producing a net saving of 8 units on the supplied account. Other location factors remain outside the calculation.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical region attracts assembly plants but imports all specialised inputs and sends profits to owners elsewhere. Explain why job growth alone does not describe the full local development effect.
questions.hint: Trace wages, local supplier links and ownership income separately.
hints: Trace wages, local supplier links and ownership income separately.
Some value can leave the region.
questions.answer: Assembly jobs can provide wages, but imported inputs limit local supplier demand and externally paid profits reduce income retained locally. Evaluate wages, skills, working conditions and local linkages alongside employment counts.

notes.title: Clustering can create savings and extra costs
paragraphs: Industrial location decisions balance transport costs, labour, infrastructure and access to markets or specialised knowledge. Agglomeration can reduce costs through shared suppliers and labour pools, but congestion, expensive land and pollution can create diseconomies as a cluster grows. A firm may relocate one production stage while retaining research or management elsewhere, producing a spatial division of labour. The resulting jobs do not necessarily capture equal shares of product value. Evaluate a production network by tracing functions and bargaining relationships, then consider wages, working conditions and local linkages rather than treating factory presence alone as complete development.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical manufacturer compares sites A and B. A saves 10 cost units through nearby suppliers but adds 14 through land and congestion; B has neither change relative to the reference. Compare the stated net effect.
steps: A’s agglomeration saving is 10, but its extra land and congestion costs total 14.
Net effect = 14 − 10 = 4 additional cost units relative to B.
workedExamples.conclusion: The cluster is not cheapest on these supplied costs, though unmeasured skills or market benefits could change the decision.

flashcards.back: Spatial clustering of economic activities with potential shared benefits.
Congestion, high land costs or concentrated pollution.

flashcards.front: What is a spatial division of labour?
flashcards.back: Different production functions located in different places.

flashcards.front: Does a local factory capture all product value?
flashcards.back: No; design, ownership and other stages may capture different shares.

diagrams.title: Clustering can create savings and extra costs
diagrams.description: The location decision compares both sides of the cost account.

nodes.label: Net supplied effect
nodes.detail: 4 additional units at the clustered site
